title: Daedalus and Icarus
text:
Daedalus, the great craftsman of Athens, was trapped on Crete by King Minos, who would not let him leave. Land and sea were guarded, but the sky was not. So Daedalus set to work making wings. He laid feathers in rows from small to large, tied them with thread at the middle and fixed them with wax at the base, and bent them gently to curve like a bird's.

His young son Icarus stood beside him, laughing, catching at floating feathers and pressing the soft wax with his thumb, getting in his father's way.

When the wings were ready, Daedalus fitted them to the boy and gave him careful instructions: fly the middle course. If you fly too low, the spray of the sea will weigh down your wings; if you fly too high, the sun will burn them. Follow me. His cheeks were wet as he spoke, and his hands trembled.

They rose into the air. Fishermen and shepherds below stared up at them, taking them for gods. But Icarus began to delight in the flight and left his father behind, soaring higher toward the sky. The heat of the sun softened the wax. The feathers fell away, and Icarus, flapping bare arms, fell into the sea calling his father's name. Daedalus found the feathers on the waves and buried his son.
lesson: Giving children freedom means trusting them with limits they may ignore. Explain the reasons for the middle course, then fly close enough to help.
